summary: Defines a way for LDP routers to advertise optional enhancements when a session starts. As new features are proposed, this lets peers learn what the other supports.

plainLanguage.summary: Two routers meeting can say which extra tricks they know. This note adds a way for them to share that list when they first connect.

subtitle: How LDP routers announce optional features when a session starts, and switch them on or off later.

tldr.problem: Many enhancements to the Label Distribution Protocol had been proposed, and LDP peers had no uniform way to tell each other which ones they support.
tldr.mechanism: A Capability Parameter TLV carried in the Initialization message advertises a capability, and a new Capability message can advertise or withdraw capabilities after the session is up.
tldr.outcome: New LDP features can define a code point and rules for their own capability, and peers that do not understand one can ignore it or end the session depending on the U-bit.

today: RFC 5561 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2009. It updates RFC 5036 and, according to the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why LDP Needs Capabilities
sections.content:
Many enhancements to LDP as specified in RFC 5036 had been proposed, including Graceful Restart, Fault Tolerant LDP, multicast extensions, signaling for Layer 2 circuits and upstream label allocation. More were expected. This document defines a way to advertise them at session initialization, and to enable and disable them after the session is established.

Capability advertisement lets an LDP speaker announce what it can receive and process, and tell peers about deviations from base behavior. Not every enhancement needs it: upstream label allocation does, but inbound label filtering does not.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers keep learning new tricks. They need a polite way to say which tricks they know before they start working together.

sections.title: The Capability Mechanism
sections.content:
Each speaker implements a set of enhancements, each with an associated capability, and may have none, one or several enabled. Advertising a capability asserts that the speaker will perform the protocol actions for that enhancement; without the advertisement it will not.

At session setup, a speaker MAY advertise a capability by including an optional parameter for it in its Initialization message. A well-known capability, Dynamic Capability Announcement, tells the peer that the speaker can process capability announcements after setup. If a peer advertised it, a speaker MAY send a Capability message at any time listing capabilities being advertised or withdrawn. For example, when an operator enables a feature, the router advertises the capability, and when the feature is disabled it withdraws it.

A document that defines an enhancement needing a capability has to describe its motivation, its behavior (procedures, parameters, messages and TLVs), and an IANA section requesting a code point from the TLV Type namespace. It must also describe how any capability data is interpreted.
sections.plainLanguage: When routers first meet, each shows a list of its tricks. If one learns a new trick later, it can add it to the list, but only if the other said it can read updates.

sections.title: The Capability Parameter TLV
sections.content:
A Capability Parameter is an optional parameter in Initialization and Capability messages. Its fields are:

  • U: the unknown-TLV bit from RFC 5036, set to 0 or 1 as the capability's own document says.
  • F: the forward-unknown bit, which MUST be 0 because these messages are not forwarded.
  • TLV Code Point: the IANA-assigned type identifying the capability.
  • Length, then the S bit, 1 to advertise and 0 to withdraw.
  • Capability Data: any extra information, interpreted as the capability's document says.

A speaker MUST NOT include the same Capability Parameter twice in one message. A receiver that sees duplicates SHOULD send a Notification with status Malformed TLV value, containing the second duplicate, before ending the session.

Backward Compatibility TLVs are older ad hoc TLVs in the Initialization message, such as the FT Session TLV for Fault Tolerance. Their presence means the same as a Capability Parameter with the S-bit set.
sections.plainLanguage: Each trick on the list is a small labeled card. One part says which trick, and one part says whether it is being turned on or off.

sections.title: The Capability Message
sections.content:
The Capability message, with code point 0x0202, announces changes in the state of one or more capabilities after the session starts. It carries a Message ID followed by one or more Capability Parameter TLVs, and the S-bit of each says the new state.

Backward Compatibility TLVs MUST NOT appear in a Capability message. A receiver SHOULD silently ignore any that do and keep processing the rest.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a short note that says: I now do this trick, or I stopped doing that one.

sections.title: Procedures at Setup and Afterwards
sections.content:
In an Initialization message the S-bit MUST be 1 and SHOULD be ignored on receipt, so any parameter there enables the capability. A speaker learns what a peer supports from the Capability Parameters in the peer's Initialization message and may use a capability once the peer has enabled it. A speaker MAY advertise a capability to a peer that does not; whether it is usable then depends on the enhancement, and its document MUST say what happens, including whether to end the session.

The U-bit decides what a receiver does with a capability it does not understand. With U=1 it MUST silently ignore the parameter and let the session come up. With U=0 it SHOULD send a Notification with status code Unsupported Capability and terminate the session.

A speaker MUST NOT send a Capability message unless the peer advertised Dynamic Capability Announcement in its Initialization. It then tracks the peer's enabled set by applying each Capability message to the set from initialization.
sections.plainLanguage: If a router does not know a trick, a flag on the card says either to just ignore it or to say sorry and stop working together.

sections.title: Errors and the Dynamic Capability TLV
sections.content:
This document defines the status code Unsupported Capability, whose Status TLV E-bit MUST be 0, and a new TLV called Returned TLVs for Notification messages. When reporting an unsupported capability, the Notification MUST include Returned TLVs containing only the unsupported Capability Parameters, SHOULD encoded as received. The same TLV carries the unknown TLV when the status code is Unknown TLV.

The Dynamic Capability Announcement TLV has U=1 and length 1, and no capability data. A speaker MAY include it in an Initialization message, MUST NOT include it in a Capability message, and cannot disable it once enabled, so its S-bit is always 1.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router refuses a trick, it sends the offending card back so the other side can see exactly which one caused the problem.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
An RFC 5036 compliant peer is treated as having label distribution for IPv4 enabled by default. Implementations with capability advertisement keep it enabled until explicitly disabled and MUST assume their peers do too. Backward Compatibility TLVs let existing enhancements keep their ad hoc way of enabling features.

The security considerations are the same as those of base LDP and of the MPLS security framework. The document adds no new ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Older routers that never heard of the list still work, because everyone assumes the basic trick is already switched on.
